passages.t: The bronze altar, and a basin made from mirrors
passages.happening:
“Bezalel constructed the altar of burnt offering from acacia wood. It was square, five cubits long, five cubits wide, and three cubits high. He made a horn at each of its four corners, so that the horns and altar were of one piece, and he overlaid the altar with bronze” (verses 1-2). Its tools, its grate and its poles are bronze (verses 3-7). “He made the altar with boards so that it was hollow” (verse 7).

“Next he made the bronze basin and its stand from the mirrors of the women who served at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
The building has moved from the tent (chapter 36) to its golden furniture (chapter 37). Now it moves out to the courtyard, where ordinary Israelites would bring their offerings.

The altar follows the plan of 27:1-8, and the note there describes it. It was a hollow box of wood covered in bronze, about 7.5 feet square and 4.5 feet high, light enough to carry on poles. It stood just inside the gate. It was the first thing a worshiper met. The layout itself taught that no one came near God's presence without passing the place of sacrifice.

Altars with horns at their corners are well known from ancient Israel. A large one of cut stones was found at Tel Beersheba in 1973, its blocks reused in a later wall.

Verse 8 holds a detail found nowhere in the plans. The bronze basin, where the priests would wash, was made from mirrors. A mirror in that world was a disk of polished bronze or copper, often with a decorated handle, and it was a prized thing to own. The women who served at the entrance to the tent gave theirs.

Who were these women, and what did they do? The text does not explain. They are mentioned only once more in the Bible. The Hebrew verb for their service is the one used for service in an army and, later, for the duties of the Levites. It suggests ordered, regular duty. More than that cannot be said.

What can be said is that the thing they once used to look at themselves became the thing in which the priests washed before they came near to God.
passages.later:
The women appear once more, in the dark days of Eli's sons, who wronged “the women who served at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting” (1 Samuel 2:22).

Hebrews says of the altar, “We have an altar from which those who serve at the tabernacle have no right to eat” (Hebrews 13:10). The note on Exodus 27 says more about how Hebrews reads the altar.
passages.asks: The women gave their mirrors for the basin. Ask what you prize that could be given to God's service. And ask whether you spend more care on how you look to others than on being clean before God.

passages.happening:
“Then he constructed the courtyard. The south side of the courtyard was a hundred cubits long and had curtains of finely spun linen, with twenty posts and twenty bronze bases, and with silver hooks and bands on the posts” (verses 9-10). The north side matches it. The west side is fifty cubits, and so is the east, “toward the sunrise” (verses 11-13).

“The curtain for the entrance to the courtyard was embroidered with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely spun linen. It was twenty cubits long” (verse 18). “All the tent pegs for the tabernacle and for the surrounding courtyard were bronze” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
The courtyard follows the plan of 27:9-19. It was about 150 by 75 feet, closed in by linen curtains about 7.5 feet high. That was high enough to block the view of anyone walking past.

There was one way in: a gate on the east, twenty cubits wide, marked by a curtain in the same colors as the veil inside.

So the camp's ordinary life went on outside the white wall. Inside were sacrifice and worship.

The metals now reach their outer edge. Across these chapters they go down in value as the work moves outward: gold for the furniture within, silver under the walls of the tent, bronze for the courtyard.
passages.later:
The psalms long for these courts: “better is one day in Your courts than a thousand elsewhere. I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God than dwell in the tents of the wicked” (Psalm 84:10).

Jesus said, “I am the gate. If anyone enters through Me, he will be saved” (John 10:9). He is speaking of a sheepfold, not of the tabernacle, so the link is one of theme.
passages.asks: The courtyard had one gate, open toward the sunrise. Ask whether you come into God's presence as someone glad to be let in. And ask whether, like the psalm-writer, you would take the lowest place in God's house over a high place anywhere else.

passages.happening:
“This is the inventory for the tabernacle, the tabernacle of the Testimony, as recorded at Moses’ command by the Levites under the direction of Ithamar son of Aaron the priest” (verse 21). Bezalel and Oholiab are named as the makers (verses 22-23).

“All the gold from the wave offering used for the work on the sanctuary totaled 29 talents and 730 shekels” (verse 24). The silver from the census came to 100 talents and 1,775 shekels, half a shekel from each of 603,550 men (verses 25-26). “With the 1,775 shekels of silver he made the hooks for the posts, overlaid their tops, and supplied bands for them” (verse 28). “The bronze from the wave offering totaled 70 talents and 2,400 shekels” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
The chapter stops building and counts. This is an accounting report, the kind of record that those who ran ancient temples kept. Everything given is written down, and what it was used for.

It may seem a dry way to end. But it matters that it is here. The people gave freely, and the leaders show openly what became of every gift. Ithamar, Aaron's youngest son, oversees the record, and the Levites keep it. Bezalel and Oholiab are named again, as if signing the finished work.

The figures agree with one another. Half a shekel from 603,550 men comes to 301,775 shekels, which the text gives as 100 talents and 1,775 shekels. So a talent here is 3,000 shekels. By common estimates of the shekel's weight, that is about a ton of gold, well over three tons of silver, and more than two tons of bronze.

The silver is the ransom money of 30:11-16, the same from rich and poor. A hundred talents made the hundred bases under the frames and the veil, one talent to a base. The half shekel was called a beka. Small stone weights marked with that word have been dug up in and around Jerusalem.
passages.later:
The same total is given in the census of Numbers: “all those counted totaled 603,550” (Numbers 1:46).

Paul took the same care with the churches' gift for the poor: “we are taking great care to do what is right, not only in the eyes of the Lord, but also in the eyes of men” (2 Corinthians 8:21).

Jesus said, “Whoever is faithful with very little will also be faithful with much” (Luke 16:10).
passages.hard:
Were there really 603,550 men of fighting age?

The number is repeated in Numbers 1:46, and it is close to the round 600,000 of Exodus 12:37. With women and children it implies two million people or more. Many readers find that hard to fit with life in the wilderness.

Readers take it in several ways. Some take the number as written and see God's provision as explanation enough. Others note that the Hebrew word elef, usually ‘thousand’, can also mean a clan or a military unit, so that the true company would be far smaller. That reading has to explain why the totals in this chapter add up as thousands. Others see the numbers as symbolic, or as a later census set back in the wilderness years. As the text stands, verses 25 and 26 show that the writer means thousands.

Each reading has its difficulty. Christians who hold Scripture as God's word are found on more than one side, and these notes take no side. What the chapter teaches does not hang on the answer: God's house stood on the ransom of every person counted, and every gift was accounted for.
passages.asks: Every gift was counted and its use recorded. Ask whether you handle what others have trusted to you, money, time or responsibility, in a way you would be glad to have written down. And ask whether you are faithful in the small things no one checks.
